And decided keyboards were obsolete.

Wispr Flow.

Silicon Valley insiders using it daily before Series A even began.

$81M raised.

Some founders build companies.

This one chose the second.

gen1.text:
I've seen Tanay Kothari on my feed about 100+ times in this week.

Usually, when a founder goes this viral, it's a PR stunt.
But looking at his actual track record, this is just pure brute force engineering.

The timeline is honestly exhausting to even read:

• Age 11: Builds a voice assistant, hits 2.5M users, Google shuts it down.
• Age 13: Learns 20 programming languages.
• Age 21: Teaches Deep Learning at Stanford with Andrew Ng.
• Rejects YC to sell his first company.

But here is the part most people are missing in the threads today.

He didn't just win constantly.
He spent years building a hardware brain-computer interface (Wispr).
It was hard. The hardware game is brutal.

He realized the software was the real bottleneck.
So he killed the hardware.
Pivoted entirely to Flow (voice dictation).
Onboarded the first 500 users personally on Google Meet.

Now he's sitting on $81M in funding and a $700M valuation because he wasn't afraid to kill his "baby" to build what actually worked.

The "overnight success" you're seeing on your timeline today is actually just a guy who has been shipping since he was 11 years old.

If you're looking for a sign to stop overthinking and start building, this is it.

It's embarrassing: A tiny startup is doing Siri's job better than Siri.

Siri still can't type a proper sentence because getting anything shipped inside a company that big requires so many approvals that the product dies before it reaches you.

A Stanford dropout with a tiny team is now shipping better voice AI than a three trillion dollar company.

Siri had every advantage you could ask for. The data, budget, distribution, and hardware integration. It is still lost to a startup, and that tells you everything about what happens when speed meets bureaucracy.

Not only does Wispr Flow work better than Siri, Apple genuinely cannot move fast enough to catch up even if they wanted to. That's what happens when bureaucracy becomes the product.

@tankots built his fourth startup and pivoted from neural interface hardware to voice dictation software. In less than a year, his team made Siri look like it hasn't been updated since 2011.

The problem was always speed and never size. 

This post is sponsored, but I genuinely love WisprFlow and use it every day (including for the first draft of this post).

gen1.text:
This is why I think Apple fucked up with Siri, big time. 

They had every resource to fix Siri. 
They just… didn’t.

If you have an accent or switch between languages, forget it. If you want it to actually understand what context you’re talking in, absolutely forget it.

“Let me look that up for you” is not only a meme, it’s a felt pain. every single time. 

Dictation has been on every device for over a decade. And it’s still barely usable. 

Everybody on here knows the way we input text is broken. We think at a speed that’s 8 times faster than typing 

Be it code, texts, context

We know it’s flawed. 

I’m genuinely posting here that Wispr Flow just fixed it. 

Not because it’s another trending AI tool. 

Because it’s actually usable by all of us. 100+ Languages and accents. It gets it all- the stuff Apple’s had a decade to figure out and still fumbles.

You speak. And it actually writes the way YOU write. Your tone. Your style. Like you sat down and typed it yourself.

This is what happens when someone actually builds for how real people talk. Not just how one demographic in Cupertino talks.

gen1.text:
Wispr raised $81M at a $700M valuation in November. They hit $10M in revenue by October 2025 with a team under 50 people growing 40% month over month.

The "3x more accurate" claim needs unpacking. One independent benchmark put Wispr at 97.2% transcription accuracy versus 85-90% for Apple Dictation and 89-92% for Google Voice Typing. But Wispr's CEO measures a different metric entirely: the percentage of messages users send without making any edits. That accounts for tone, formatting, and context, like spelling "Bryan" correctly based on your contacts or adjusting formality between Slack and email. Edit-free output rate is a harder bar than word error rate, and it's the one that determines whether someone keeps using the product or goes back to typing.

This tells you everything about why Apple, Microsoft, and Google have failed here. They've bundled voice dictation free into every OS for over a decade. Nobody uses it, because 90% accuracy means a mistake in nearly every sentence. Users learn to associate voice input with frustration, and that association is almost impossible to reverse through incremental improvement. Wispr charges $12/month and 270 Fortune 500 companies are paying, which means the habit-formation threshold sits somewhere between 90% and 97%. Below that line, free isn't cheap enough. Above it, people will pay.

The average B2B SaaS company spends $702 to acquire a customer. At $12/month, that's a 4.8 year payback before churn. Paid acquisition breaks at a $144/year price point, which is why most PLG companies at this tier (Notion, Figma early days, Superhuman) lean on organic loops.

Wispr's is extreme even by those standards. 90% of growth is word of mouth. Kothari personally onboarded the first 500 users over Google Meet, watching facial expressions and mouse movements to find exact moments of delight, then engineered those moments into the product. He killed SEO entirely because "no one is searching for voice dictation." You can't run demand capture on a category most people assume is still broken. The Porsche challenge is the same logic at scale: a $250K product demo that shifts perception of a category written off for a decade.

Wispr was also the 8th product the team built internally. The first 7 were computer action tools similar to what OpenAI later shipped as Operator. People used them once a day if they remembered. Voice dictation stuck because people spend 90% of computer time consuming content or communicating. Massive surface area for a habit-forming input tool at $12/month.

The $700M valuation prices in a question. The organic loop works because the product is visible: someone dictating in a meeting generates curiosity. But that loop was built inside Silicon Valley, where every VC was already a daily user before the Series A. Kothari has said 95% of the population is the real market. The Android launch today and the enterprise push (125 new companies per week as of November) are both attempts to answer whether word-of-mouth scales when the early network stops being San Francisco tech workers.

Tanay Kothari didn’t just announce @WisprFlow  .

Break it.
Test it.
Prove it wrong.

Now founders are doing the opposite.

Ship in public.
Invite scrutiny.
Let the product defend itself.

That’s why this angle is spreading so quickly.
Because the new distribution strategy isn’t ads.
It’s founder conviction + public testing.

We’re going to see a lot more launches like this. 🚀

/1 I've been testing voice-first writing more seriously lately. Not casually, but as a legit workflow upgrade.

And it's already flipping how I work.

When dictation gets fast + accurate + zero lag, the keyboard just stops being default. You're not forcing thoughts through fingers anymore. You're capturing them at real speaking speed. That shift compounds insanely quick.

Ties straight into where AI is headed. Agents + voice modes (like in Claude, ChatGPT, or new tools like Typeless) are making expression cost nothing. Rambling? Exposed instantly. Weak ideas? Obvious right away. Editing becomes the craft. Drafting is basically free.

Energy changes too. Speaking flows unrestricted. Ideas balloon, you chase threads you'd skip because it's effortless. Same reason agentic coding exploded since December. No more line-by-line typing, just English tasks + parallel review. Voice is the next layer: thoughts at human speed, grounded in frontier models.

This rewrites white-collar creation. Emails, threads, docs. Weeks shrink to minutes. Keyboard lingers, but it might stop owning the center. Way more people switching soon, very soon.

2027404378307809701.text:
Speaking is faster than typing. That’s why using speech AI is a hack.

From my debate days, I could speak at 281 WPM with 100% accuracy. But I’m so used to autocorrect that my typing was not only slow, it was inaccurate. 281 WPM dictation. 28 WPM typing. A 10x difference on the same person, producing the same output.

The average knowledge worker types at 40 WPM. Speaking speed averages 150 WPM. That’s a 3.75x gap between how fast you think and how fast you can get thoughts into a machine.

The keyboard has been the bottleneck for every knowledge worker for 50 years. We accepted it because built-in dictation was so bad it created more work than it saved. You’d spend 30 seconds dictating and 2 minutes fixing transcription errors.

What changed is the AI layer between your voice and the text field. Tools like Wispr Flow don’t just transcribe. They understand intent, strip filler words, and format contextually. The error correction problem that killed voice input for decades just disappeared.

Thanks to Wispr Flow for partnering on this post. I genuinely use it every day for drafting PRDs, writing newsletter content, and responding to Slack. It’s become invisible infrastructure in my workflow.

Think about what this means for daily output. A PM writing a PRD at 40 WPM spends 60-90 minutes typing a 3,000-word doc. At 4x speed with voice, that’s 15-22 minutes for the same output. A founder answering 50 emails a day reclaims an hour. A content creator producing 5,000 words of newsletter copy cuts a full morning down to 45 minutes.

The people who figure out the input layer first will simply produce more. More docs, more content, more decisions communicated clearly. Speed of output is a compounding advantage in knowledge work, and we’ve been leaving a 4-10x multiplier on the table because the keyboard felt “good enough.”

Try the challenge. You’ll see the gap instantly.

quoted_tweet.text:
Wispr raised $81M at a $700M valuation in November. They hit $10M in revenue by October 2025 with a team under 50 people growing 40% month over month.

The "3x more accurate" claim needs unpacking. One independent benchmark put Wispr at 97.2% transcription accuracy versus 85-90% for Apple Dictation and 89-92% for Google Voice Typing. But Wispr's CEO measures a different metric entirely: the percentage of messages users send without making any edits. That accounts for tone, formatting, and context, like spelling "Bryan" correctly based on your contacts or adjusting formality between Slack and email. Edit-free output rate is a harder bar than word error rate, and it's the one that determines whether someone keeps using the product or goes back to typing.

This tells you everything about why Apple, Microsoft, and Google have failed here. They've bundled voice dictation free into every OS for over a decade. Nobody uses it, because 90% accuracy means a mistake in nearly every sentence. Users learn to associate voice input with frustration, and that association is almost impossible to reverse through incremental improvement. Wispr charges $12/month and 270 Fortune 500 companies are paying, which means the habit-formation threshold sits somewhere between 90% and 97%. Below that line, free isn't cheap enough. Above it, people will pay.

The average B2B SaaS company spends $702 to acquire a customer. At $12/month, that's a 4.8 year payback before churn. Paid acquisition breaks at a $144/year price point, which is why most PLG companies at this tier (Notion, Figma early days, Superhuman) lean on organic loops.

Wispr's is extreme even by those standards. 90% of growth is word of mouth. Kothari personally onboarded the first 500 users over Google Meet, watching facial expressions and mouse movements to find exact moments of delight, then engineered those moments into the product. He killed SEO entirely because "no one is searching for voice dictation." You can't run demand capture on a category most people assume is still broken. The Porsche challenge is the same logic at scale: a $250K product demo that shifts perception of a category written off for a decade.

Wispr was also the 8th product the team built internally. The first 7 were computer action tools similar to what OpenAI later shipped as Operator. People used them once a day if they remembered. Voice dictation stuck because people spend 90% of computer time consuming content or communicating. Massive surface area for a habit-forming input tool at $12/month.

The $700M valuation prices in a question. The organic loop works because the product is visible: someone dictating in a meeting generates curiosity. But that loop was built inside Silicon Valley, where every VC was already a daily user before the Series A. Kothari has said 95% of the population is the real market. The Android launch today and the enterprise push (125 new companies per week as of November) are both attempts to answer whether word-of-mouth scales when the early network stops being San Francisco tech workers.

Usually, when a founder goes this viral, it's a PR stunt.

He didn't just win constantly.
He spent years building a hardware brain-computer interface (Wispr).
It was hard. The hardware game is brutal.

He realized the software was the real bottleneck.
So he killed the hardware.
Pivoted entirely to Flow (voice dictation).
Onboarded the first 500 users personally on Google Meet.

Now he's sitting on $81M in funding and a $700M valuation because he wasn't afraid to kill his "baby" to build what actually worked.

The "overnight success" you're seeing on your timeline today is actually just a guy who has been shipping since he was 11 years old.

If you're looking for a sign to stop overthinking and start building, this is it.

Voice and AI assistants are already a rocket ship. The global voice AI market was ~$7.35 billion in 2024 and the general AI assistant market is poised to hit $73.8 billion by 2033. These numbers represent a thesis -> even if Wispr captures a sliver of the pie, it is already sitting at a billion-dollar opportunity... at minimum.

Now, consider this.

Wispr is a habit-forming product. The fascinating part isn’t the funding. It’s the behavior shift. People who think Wispr is “another dictation app" missed the point.

Microsoft and Google shipped dictation apps for a decade. Apple bundled it into mac and iOS for free. Still, nobody used it. Why? Because they get to 85-90% accuracy. 90% accuracy means you're editing almost every sentence you speak. That's frustrating.

Wispr got 97.2% accuracy and baked in the context about who YOU are. It types "Bryan" not "Brian" based on your contacts. The tone shifts from casual in Slack to formal in email. After 3 months, users type 50% of their content via voice. After 6 months it's 72%.

What really gets me excited is where Tanay is steering this. In interviews I watched, he kept emphasizing that Wispr’s goal isn’t just transcription > it’s true understanding. He talks about building an assistant that “doesn’t just listen, but acts.”

Now layer on the Android launch.

That's where it gets asymmetric.

Until today, Wispr hadn't even scratched the Android user market - 54.6% of global mobile users. Their custom-built Hinglish model is ripe for adoption by 600 million+ users in India itself. While other SaaS companies spend around $702/user, Wispr is growing 90% word-of-mouth. That's as massive as it gets for a habit-forming tool at $12/month. This potentially makes Wispr a default input layer for emerging markets.

The DPS RKP mafia joke is funny.

But zoom out.

A kid obsessed with building Jarvis. Stanford AI background. Multiple startups before 25. Patience to work on a single problem long enough. Now building a company that might redefine how people interact with computers.

If voice becomes default over the next decade, Wispr won't be "a startup." It'll be infrastructure. And if that happens, we'll look back at this phase — sub-unicorn, sub-100 employees — and realize the signals were obvious.

Tanay now plays in the same leagues as the other legends from DPS RKP - Raghuram Rajan. Vineeta Singh. Kunal Bahl. Rohit Bansal.

Some people peak in school.
Some people just start there.

That's DPS RKP mafia for you.

Wispr raised $81M at a $700M valuation in November. They hit $10M in revenue by October 2025 with a team under 50 people growing 40% month over month.

The "3x more accurate" claim needs unpacking. One independent benchmark put Wispr at 97.2% transcription accuracy versus 85-90% for Apple Dictation and 89-92% for Google Voice Typing. But Wispr's CEO measures a different metric entirely: the percentage of messages users send without making any edits. That accounts for tone, formatting, and context, like spelling "Bryan" correctly based on your contacts or adjusting formality between Slack and email. Edit-free output rate is a harder bar than word error rate, and it's the one that determines whether someone keeps using the product or goes back to typing.

This tells you everything about why Apple, Microsoft, and Google have failed here. They've bundled voice dictation free into every OS for over a decade. Nobody uses it, because 90% accuracy means a mistake in nearly every sentence. Users learn to associate voice input with frustration, and that association is almost impossible to reverse through incremental improvement. Wispr charges $12/month and 270 Fortune 500 companies are paying, which means the habit-formation threshold sits somewhere between 90% and 97%. Below that line, free isn't cheap enough. Above it, people will pay.

The average B2B SaaS company spends $702 to acquire a customer. At $12/month, that's a 4.8 year payback before churn. Paid acquisition breaks at a $144/year price point, which is why most PLG companies at this tier (Notion, Figma early days, Superhuman) lean on organic loops.

Wispr's is extreme even by those standards. 90% of growth is word of mouth. Kothari personally onboarded the first 500 users over Google Meet, watching facial expressions and mouse movements to find exact moments of delight, then engineered those moments into the product. He killed SEO entirely because "no one is searching for voice dictation." You can't run demand capture on a category most people assume is still broken. The Porsche challenge is the same logic at scale: a $250K product demo that shifts perception of a category written off for a decade.

Wispr was also the 8th product the team built internally. The first 7 were computer action tools similar to what OpenAI later shipped as Operator. People used them once a day if they remembered. Voice dictation stuck because people spend 90% of computer time consuming content or communicating. Massive surface area for a habit-forming input tool at $12/month.

The $700M valuation prices in a question. The organic loop works because the product is visible: someone dictating in a meeting generates curiosity.
